content: The total square footage of the hospital wing containing the laboratories was obtained from surveyor reports provided by the financial director. The annual number of tests performed in each laboratory was reported by the senior microbiologist. Case Study 3: Personnel Time in Indonesia The staff costs associated with IGRA tests in Indonesia were calculated through interviews with resident doctors who collected blood samples from patients in the clinic and through time-motion studies observing laboratory technicians performing analyses in an immunology laboratory. The resident doctors were asked about patient flow in the clinic and were requested to estimate the time required for a full patient consultation, including IGRA-specific activities such as explaining the test and drawing blood. Data on the total monthly working hours, the number of patients seen at the clinic, and the number of patients receiving IGRA tests were obtained from the clinic’s supervising doctor. In the immunology laboratory, the laboratory doctor was briefed on the study’s objectives and methodology, which aimed to determine the unit costs of tuberculosis (TB) screening and diagnostic tests at a teaching hospital in West Java, Indonesia. The laboratory doctor facilitated a meeting with two laboratory technicians who analyzed the blood samples. During this meeting, the technicians were also briefed on the study’s objectives and costing methodology. They explained the workflow of the analysis, the equipment used, and the challenges associated with IGRA tests, particularly in maintaining the quality of blood samples during collection, transportation, and laboratory processing. The technicians were then asked to participate in a time-motion study to document the time taken for each task, as well as the consumables, chemicals, and reagents used. Since the IGRA test was newly implemented at the facility (within the past year), the volume of samples was inconsistent and insufficient for daily analysis. As a result, analyses were conducted in batches, typically at the end of the week. The time-motion study was scheduled for the following Friday. On the day of the study, the technicians reviewed a diagram of the sample workflow and a list of IGRA-relevant equipment, consumables, chemicals, and reagents that had been created after the initial meeting. Adjustments were made to the workflow and lists as necessary, and each task was numbered sequentially. During the time-motion study, the observer positioned themselves in a corner of the laboratory with a clear view of the processes involved in sample analysis. As the technicians performed each task, the observer used a digital stopwatch to record the time for each task and took notes on the activities, equipment, and consumables used. The entire analysis process was timed and annotated without interacting with the technicians. Waiting times and the recording of results were also included in the study. After the study, the technician reviewed the workflow again and filled in any gaps regarding the process, equipment, consumables, chemicals, or reagents. The time-motion study was repeated the following Friday with a more junior technician. The average time taken to perform an IGRA test analysis was used to calculate the unit costs. Ethical Considerations Before engaging with clinicians or laboratory staff, approval letters from the ethics review committee and permission letters were provided to the clinic and laboratory supervisors. The time required for sample administration (delivery to the laboratory, storage, and disposal after analysis) was obtained through interviews with the laboratory doctor and technicians, as these processes did not occur simultaneously with the analysis and could not be included in the time-motion study. Study Overview and Consent Process The study, titled Costing the Delivery of Tuberculosis Services in [Country Name] from a Health Systems’ Perspective, was conducted by [Lead Institution Name] in collaboration with the Ministry of Health’s National Tuberculosis Programme and other collaborators. The research aimed to estimate the costs of providing TB services and to develop a comprehensive set of unit costs for TB services in the country. The study involved interviews with key staff members, document reviews, observations, and timesheets completed by staff. Participation in the study was voluntary, and participants could withdraw at any time without consequences. The study posed no major risks, and all responses and observations were treated confidentially. The data collected would be anonymized and aggregated to estimate the unit cost per TB episode. The findings would be shared in summary form with participating facilities, the National TB Programme, and the wider scientific community to improve TB services and resource planning. Data Security and Sharing All documents were securely stored in locked cabinets and password-protected computers. Anonymized data would be shared with the Global Health Cost Consortium (GHCC) to improve cost extrapolations across settings. The cost data would also be incorporated into the GHCC’s web-based platform. Informed Consent Participants were provided with detailed explanations of the study and had the opportunity to ask questions.
